title: Lesson 6: Hiring, Onboarding, and Running a Team of Consultants
description: The principal hires for the delivery system, not for a role they used to fill. How to staff against a captured method, onboard people onto it with a measurable exit gate, and run a team so quality stays a property of the system instead of a bet on any single person.

questions.question: What should a principal actually hire for?
options: Prior experience with the exact tooling and a strong individual track record.
The ability to fill the role the principal used to hold personally.
A slot in the delivery method: faithfulness to it plus judgment where it does not cover.
Willingness to work long hours and take on every kind of task.
questions.explanation: The role is a slot in a captured method, so the two things to evaluate are whether the person runs the playbook as built and whether they flag the moments it does not cover instead of improvising past them.

questions.question: What does the onboarding exit gate require before a new hire is finished?
options: Comfort with the team and familiarity with the tools.
The ability to run a defined engagement arc to standard, behind review gates, without the principal touching a deliverable.
Completion of a fixed reading list and a written exam.
A signed acknowledgment that the method has been read.
questions.explanation: Onboarding ends with a measurable gate, not a feeling: the hire can run the engagement arc to the same standard any engagement must meet, with the principal only reading health reports.

questions.question: What is the key-person trap, and how is it remedied?
options: One consultant is the only one who can run a critical offer, and the remedy is cross-training so capability is held by the system.
The principal works too many hours, and the remedy is delegating the least important tasks.
A new hire ramps too slowly, and the remedy is a longer probation period.
The team depends on one client, and the remedy is signing more clients.
questions.explanation: If a capability lives in one person, the practice rents rather than owns it, so every sold capability needs more than one person who can run it, held by the method and the system instead.
